claim: The fertilised zygote undergoes a series of cleavage divisions and morphogenetic events that give rise to a blastocyst over the first 5 days of human development.
source: Over the first 5 days of human development, the fertilised zygote undergoes a series of cleavage divisions and morphogenetic events that give rise to a blastocyst, which comprises an inner cell mass (ICM) and a fluid-filled cavity surrounded by the trophoblast, the extra-embryonic tissue that forms the placenta (Edwards et al., 1970; Steptoe et al., 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 1970 and Steptoe et al., 1971, which are referenced as the source of this information.

claim: The blastocyst comprises an inner cell mass (ICM) and a fluid-filled cavity surrounded by the trophoblast.
source: Over the first 5 days of human development, the fertilised zygote undergoes a series of cleavage divisions and morphogenetic events that give rise to a blastocyst, which comprises an inner cell mass (ICM) and a fluid-filled cavity surrounded by the trophoblast, the extra-embryonic tissue that forms the placenta (Edwards et al., 1970; Steptoe et al., 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 1970 and Steptoe et al., 1971.

claim: The trophoblast is the extra-embryonic tissue that forms the placenta.
source: Over the first 5 days of human development, the fertilised zygote undergoes a series of cleavage divisions and morphogenetic events that give rise to a blastocyst, which comprises an inner cell mass (ICM) and a fluid-filled cavity surrounded by the trophoblast, the extra-embryonic tissue that forms the placenta (Edwards et al., 1970; Steptoe et al., 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 1970 and Steptoe et al., 1971.

claim: As the blastocyst matures, the ICM undergoes a morphological sorting process which leads to the specification of the epiblast and the hypoblast.
source: As the blastocyst matures, the ICM undergoes a morphological sorting process which leads to the specification of the epiblast, progenitor of the embryo proper, and the hypoblast (extra-embryonic endoderm), the precursor tissue of the yolk sac (Wamaitha and Niakan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wamaitha and Niakan, 2018.

claim: The epiblast is the progenitor of the embryo proper.
source: As the blastocyst matures, the ICM undergoes a morphological sorting process which leads to the specification of the epiblast, progenitor of the embryo proper, and the hypoblast (extra-embryonic endoderm), the precursor tissue of the yolk sac (Wamaitha and Niakan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wamaitha and Niakan, 2018.

claim: The hypoblast (extra-embryonic endoderm) is the precursor tissue of the yolk sac.
source: As the blastocyst matures, the ICM undergoes a morphological sorting process which leads to the specification of the epiblast, progenitor of the embryo proper, and the hypoblast (extra-embryonic endoderm), the precursor tissue of the yolk sac (Wamaitha and Niakan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wamaitha and Niakan, 2018.

claim: The human blastocyst implants into the uterine wall of the mother on embryonic day 6–7 (E6–7) post-fertilisation.
source: Once the hypoblast, epiblast, and trophoblast have been specified, the human blastocyst is ready to implant into the uterine wall of the mother on embryonic day 6–7 (E6–7) post-fertilisation (Steptoe et al., 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steptoe et al., 1971.

claim: Upon implantation, epiblast cells polarise and undergo lumenogenesis to form the amniotic cavity.
source: In vivo and in vitro studies of human and non-human primates (Deglincerti et al., 2016; Luckett, 1975; Ma et al., 2019; Niu et al., 2019; Shahbazi et al., 2016) have shown that upon implantation, epiblast cells polarise and undergo lumenogenesis to form the amniotic cavity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Deglincerti et al., 2016; Luckett, 1975; Ma et al., 2019; Niu et al., 2019; Shahbazi et al., 2016).

claim: Epiblast cells located in close proximity to the hypoblast become a columnar epiblast disc, in contact with the amniotic cavity.
source: Epiblast cells located in close proximity to the hypoblast become a columnar epiblast disc, in contact with the amniotic cavity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text following the description of amniotic cavity formation, drawing from the same studies mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: The hypoblast proliferates, giving rise to the primary yolk sac on day 10.
source: The hypoblast proliferates, giving rise to the primary yolk sac on day 10.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text following the description of epiblast disc formation.

claim: Around day 14, the primitive streak forms posteriorly in the epiblast, triggering the onset of gastrulation.
source: Around day 14, the primitive streak forms posteriorly in the epiblast, triggering the onset of gastrulation (Sasaki et al., 2016; Shahbazi, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sasaki et al., 2016 and Shahbazi, 2020.

claim: In the mouse embryo, the anterior visceral endoderm (AVE) is established at E5.5.
source: In the mouse embryo, a group of asymmetrically localised cells, collectively known as the anterior visceral endoderm (AVE), is established at E5.5, which secrete NODAL, WNT, and BMP antagonists (e.g. Lefty, Dkk1, Cer1, Noggin), leading to the formation of a gradient of signalling activity across the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo (Beddington and Robertson, 1999; Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beddington and Robertson, 1999 and Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005.

claim: The anterior visceral endoderm (AVE) secretes NODAL, WNT, and BMP antagonists (e.g. Lefty, Dkk1, Cer1, Noggin).
source: In the mouse embryo, a group of asymmetrically localised cells, collectively known as the anterior visceral endoderm (AVE), is established at E5.5, which secrete NODAL, WNT, and BMP antagonists (e.g. Lefty, Dkk1, Cer1, Noggin), leading to the formation of a gradient of signalling activity across the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo (Beddington and Robertson, 1999; Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beddington and Robertson, 1999 and Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005.

claim: The AVE leads to the formation of a gradient of signalling activity across the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo.
source: In the mouse embryo, a group of asymmetrically localised cells, collectively known as the anterior visceral endoderm (AVE), is established at E5.5, which secrete NODAL, WNT, and BMP antagonists (e.g. Lefty, Dkk1, Cer1, Noggin), leading to the formation of a gradient of signalling activity across the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo (Beddington and Robertson, 1999; Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beddington and Robertson, 1999 and Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson, 2005.

claim: AVE-like cells have been identified in the cynomolgus monkey yolk sac in vivo.
source: Interestingly, AVE-like cells have also been identified in the cynomolgus monkey yolk sac in vivo (Sasaki et al., 2016), and in human embryos cultured in vitro (Molè et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sasaki et al., 2016.

claim: AVE-like cells have been identified in human embryos cultured in vitro.
source: Interestingly, AVE-like cells have also been identified in the cynomolgus monkey yolk sac in vivo (Sasaki et al., 2016), and in human embryos cultured in vitro (Molè et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Molè et al., 2021 and Xiang et al., 2020.

claim: Culture conditions now support the development of human embryos in vitro up until the internationally accepted limit of 14 days.
source: Culture conditions now support the development of human embryos in vitro up until the internationally accepted limit of 14 days (Deglincerti et al., 2016; Shahbazi et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deglincerti et al., 2016; Shahbazi et al., 2016; Xiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) have been used to model early embryogenesis.
source: Such research has already begun, with human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) being used to model early embryogenesis (Etoc et al., 2016; Moris et al., 2020; Shahbazi et al., 2017; Simunovic et al., 2019; Warmflash et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Etoc et al., 2016; Moris et al., 2020; Shahbazi et al., 2017; Simunovic et al., 2019; Warmflash et al., 2014.

claim: Current stem cell systems for modeling embryogenesis lack the inclusion of extra-embryonic tissues.
source: However, the current systems lack the inclusion of extra-embryonic tissues, which are likely key regulators of human epiblast patterning.
evidence: This claim is stated as an observation about current systems, based on the authors' assessment of the field.

claim: Extra-embryonic tissues are likely key regulators of human epiblast patterning.
source: However, the current systems lack the inclusion of extra-embryonic tissues, which are likely key regulators of human epiblast patterning.
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis based on the authors' understanding of embryonic development.

claim: The authors generated yolk sac-like cells (YSLCs) by simultaneously stimulating ACTIVIN-A, WNT, and JAK/STAT signalling in peri-implantation-like human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs).
source: To do this, we first generated yolk sac-like cells (YSLCs) by simultaneously stimulating ACTIVIN-A, WNT, and JAK/STAT signalling in peri-implantation-like human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) (Gafni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach taken by the authors, with a citation to Gafni et al., 2013 for the hPSC type used.

claim: YSLCs induce the expression of pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers at the expense of mesoderm and endoderm markers in hESCs by inhibiting BMP and WNT signalling pathways.
source: We then modelled the interaction between these YSLCs and hESCs, which revealed that YSLCs induce the expression of pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers at the expense of mesoderm and endoderm markers in hESCs by inhibiting BMP and WNT signalling pathways.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main experimental findings of the study.

claim: Conventionally, hESCs have been used as a reliable model of the human epiblast, harbouring a post-implantation, 'primed' pluripotent state.
source: Conventionally, hESCs have been used as a reliable model of the human epiblast, harbouring a post-implantation, 'primed' pluripotent state (Nakamura et al., 2016; Shao et al., 2017a; Simunovic et al., 2019; Warmflash et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2016; Shao et al., 2017a; Simunovic et al., 2019; Warmflash et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2019.

claim: Human extended pluripotent stem cells (hEPSCs) were shown to have extra-embryonic potential when incorporated into mouse embryos.
source: We hypothesised that human extended pluripotent stem cells (hEPSCs) were an appropriate candidate as they were shown to have extra-embryonic potential when incorporated into mouse embryos (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: The combination of WNT (via the GSK3 activator CHIR 99021) and ACTIVIN-A pathway activation led to the greatest upregulation of SOX17 at the expense of SOX2 after 6 days in hEPSCs.
source: By analysing SOX17 and SOX2 reporter fluorescence intensity, we discerned that the combination of WNT (via the GSK3 activator CHIR 99021) and ACTIVIN-A pathway activation led to the greatest upregulation of SOX17 at the expense of SOX2 after 6 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: ACTIVIN-A and WNT signalling are involved in the specification of mouse, monkey, and human primitive endoderm in vitro and in vivo.
source: This result is in line with ACTIVIN-A and WNT signalling being involved in the specification of mouse, monkey, and human primitive endoderm in vitro and in vivo (Anderson et al., 2017; Blakeley et al., 2015; Boroviak et al., 2015; Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2017; Blakeley et al., 2015; Boroviak et al., 2015; Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019.

claim: Human leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) is necessary for proliferation during the conversion of hEPSCs to YSLCs.
source: We further optimised the medium by increasing the concentrations of both CHIR 99021 and ACTIVIN-A (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), and removing the other cytokines from the LCDM medium apart from human leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), which we found to be necessary for proliferation during the conversion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ACL treatment on hEPSCs results in a strong shift from a SOX2 high, SOX17 low population of cells to the converse.
source: To further assess the effect of ACL treatment on hEPSCs after 6 days of culture, we analysed the expression levels of SOX17 and SOX2 using reporter fluorescence at the single cell level. This revealed a strong shift from an originally SOX2 high, SOX17 low population of cells, to the converse (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–C.

claim: Pan-endodermal markers SOX17, GATA6, and EOMES were all upregulated following ACL treatment in hEPSCs.
source: Furthermore, gene expression analysis showed that pan-endodermal markers SOX17, GATA6, and EOMES were all upregulated following ACL treatment (Figure 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Despite observed downregulation of SOX2 expression, the expression of OCT4 and NANOG increased following ACL treatment in hEPSCs.
source: Despite observed downregulation of SOX2 expression, the expression of OCT4 and NANOG increased (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which has previously been observed in hESCs overexpressing SOX17 (Séguin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, and a citation to Séguin et al., 2008.

claim: The upregulation of OCT4 and NANOG despite SOX2 downregulation has previously been observed in hESCs overexpressing SOX17.
source: Despite observed downregulation of SOX2 expression, the expression of OCT4 and NANOG increased (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which has previously been observed in hESCs overexpressing SOX17 (Séguin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Séguin et al., 2008.

claim: The inability of ACL to fully downregulate pluripotency markers in hPSCs may indicate that cells may still preserve some features of pluripotent cells.
source: The inability of ACL to fully downregulate pluripotency markers in hPSCs may indicate that cells may still preserve some features of pluripotent cells.
evidence: This claim is presented as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Rset hPSCs harbour a pluripotent state that is intermediate between pre-implantation 'ground-state' naïve pluripotency and post-implantation lineage-biased primed pluripotency.
source: To determine whether ACL could also induce endodermal fate in other hPSCs, we treated both RUES2-GLR Rset hPSCs, which harbour a pluripotent state that is intermediate between pre-implantation 'ground-state' naïve pluripotency and post-implantation lineage-biased primed pluripotency (Gafni et al., 2013; Kilens et al., 2018), and conventional primed RUES2-GLR hESCs, that are similar to the post-implantation human epiblast (Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gafni et al., 2013 and Kilens et al., 2018.

claim: Conventional primed RUES2-GLR hESCs are similar to the post-implantation human epiblast.
source: To determine whether ACL could also induce endodermal fate in other hPSCs, we treated both RUES2-GLR Rset hPSCs, which harbour a pluripotent state that is intermediate between pre-implantation 'ground-state' naïve pluripotency and post-implantation lineage-biased primed pluripotency (Gafni et al., 2013; Kilens et al., 2018), and conventional primed RUES2-GLR hESCs, that are similar to the post-implantation human epiblast (Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Molè et al., 2021 and Nakamura et al., 2016.

claim: After 6 days of ACL treatment, endodermal markers were upregulated and SOX2 was downregulated in both Rset hPSCs and hESCs.
source: After 6 days of treatment, endodermal markers were upregulated and SOX2 was downregulated in both Rset hPSCs and hESCs (Figure 1E–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E–K.

claim: The expression pattern of upregulated endodermal markers and downregulated SOX2 was also observed after 1 month of culture in ACL.
source: This expression pattern was also observed after 1 month of culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: LIF is required for continued proliferation for both Rset hPSCs and hESCs treated with ACL.
source: We also observed the requirement of LIF for continued proliferation for both of these treated hPSC populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ACL treatment using H9-derived and SHEF6-derived hEPSCs, Rset hPSCs, and hESCs revealed that SOX17, GATA6, and EOMES were upregulated after 6 days in all three populations for all cell lines at the protein and RNA level.
source: To evaluate whether these results were cell line specific, we repeated ACL treatment using H9-derived and SHEF6-derived hEPSCs, Rset hPSCs, and hESCs. This revealed a similar result, in that SOX17, GATA6, and EOMES were upregulated after 6 days in all three populations for all cell lines at the protein and RNA level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: SOX2 protein levels were downregulated upon ACL treatment in all three hPSCs for all cell lines.
source: SOX2 protein levels were also downregulated upon ACL treatment in all three hPSCs for all cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–J and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–J and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: SOX2 was upregulated at the mRNA level in treated H9 hEPSC cells.
source: However, SOX2 was upregulated at the mRNA level in treated H9 hEPSC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Single-cell fluorescence intensity analysis revealed that SOX2 upregulation at the mRNA level in H9 hEPSCs was likely due to a subpopulation of cells that were GATA6 low but expressed high SOX2 levels.
source: Single-cell fluorescence intensity analysis revealed this was likely due to a subpopulation of cells that were GATA6 low but expressed high SOX2 levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), rather than GATA6 high cells co-expressing high levels of SOX2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There is a heterogeneous response to ACL treatment within H9 hEPSCs.
source: This suggests that there is a heterogeneous response to ACL treatment within H9 hEPSCs.
evidence: This claim is presented as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: All three hPSC ACL-treated populations bore a greater similarity to the hypoblast following ACL treatment, while their similarity to the epiblast decreased.
source: This analysis revealed that all three cell populations bore a greater similarity to the hypoblast following ACL treatment, while their similarity to the epiblast decreased, suggesting a shift towards an endodermal fate (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Rset-ACL bore the greatest similarity of the three ACL-treated cell lines with the human hypoblast.
source: Interestingly, Rset-ACL bore the greatest similarity of the three ACL-treated cell lines with the human hypoblast, while hESC-ACL was the most similar of the three to the definitive endoderm (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: hESC-ACL was the most similar of the three ACL-treated cell lines to the definitive endoderm.
source: Interestingly, Rset-ACL bore the greatest similarity of the three ACL-treated cell lines with the human hypoblast, while hESC-ACL was the most similar of the three to the definitive endoderm (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: EOMES, GATA6, and SOX17 are pan-endodermal markers, which are expressed in both extra-embryonic endoderm and embryonic definitive endoderm across mammalian models.
source: EOMES, GATA6, and SOX17 are pan-endodermal markers, which are expressed in both extra-embryonic endoderm and embryonic definitive endoderm across mammalian models (Stern and Downs, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stern and Downs, 2012.

claim: 24,894 of the 26,510 genes analysed were shared by both human extra-embryonic and definitive endoderm.
source: This revealed that 24,894 of the 26,510 genes analysed were shared by both endodermal lineages, demonstrating considerable similarity between embryonic and extra-embryonic endoderm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 366 genes were found to be differentially upregulated in the definitive endoderm.
source: Nonetheless, 366 and 1250 genes were found to be differentially upregulated in the definitive endoderm and extra-embryonic endoderm, respectively (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: 1250 genes were found to be differentially upregulated in the extra-embryonic endoderm.
source: Nonetheless, 366 and 1250 genes were found to be differentially upregulated in the definitive endoderm and extra-embryonic endoderm, respectively (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Extra-embryonic endoderm markers included APOA1, APOA2, APOE, and APOC1.
source: Extra-embryonic endoderm markers included APOA1, APOA2, APOE, and APOC1 (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2) in agreement with the function of the yolk sac as the primary site of apolipoprotein synthesis during early primate, chick and mouse development (Baardman et al., 2013; Cindrova-Davies et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2, and citations to Baardman et al., 2013 and Cindrova-Davies et al., 2017.

claim: The yolk sac is the primary site of apolipoprotein synthesis during early primate, chick and mouse development.
source: Extra-embryonic endoderm markers included APOA1, APOA2, APOE, and APOC1 (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2) in agreement with the function of the yolk sac as the primary site of apolipoprotein synthesis during early primate, chick and mouse development (Baardman et al., 2013; Cindrova-Davies et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baardman et al., 2013 and Cindrova-Davies et al., 2017.

claim: PDGFRα, NID2, FN1, HNF1β, HNF4a, COL4A1, PITX2, and PODXL were identified as human extra-embryonic endoderm markers.
source: Similarly, PDGFRα, NID2, FN1, HNF1β, HNF4a, COL4A1, PITX2, and PODXL were also identified as human extra-embryonic endoderm markers (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2), in line with the mouse extra-embryonic endoderm expression profile at various stages of development (Ghatpande et al., 2002; Johansson et al., 1997; Kwon et al., 2008; Rodriguez et al., 2005; Shahbazi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2, and citations to Ghatpande et al., 2002; Johansson et al., 1997; Kwon et al., 2008; Rodriguez et al., 2005; Shahbazi et al., 2017.

claim: hESC-ACL is the most similar to human definitive endoderm of the three ACL-treated populations.
source: This revealed hESC-ACL to be the most similar to human definitive endoderm of the three populations, and Rset-ACL the most similar to extra-embryonic endoderm (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Rset-ACL is the most similar to extra-embryonic endoderm of the three ACL-treated populations.
source: This revealed hESC-ACL to be the most similar to human definitive endoderm of the three populations, and Rset-ACL the most similar to extra-embryonic endoderm (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: hEPSC-ACL were more similar to definitive endoderm than extra-embryonic endoderm.
source: hEPSC-ACL were also more similar to definitive endoderm than extra-embryonic endoderm (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The initial pluripotent state determines the endodermal fate that ACL treatment induces in hPSC populations.
source: Collectively, this transcriptional profiling of ACL-treated hPSCs indicates that the initial pluripotent state determines the endodermal fate that ACL treatment induces in hPSC populations.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The fact that primed hESCs give rise to the most definitive endoderm-like population of the three is in line with previous findings.
source: The fact that primed hESCs give rise to the most definitive endoderm-like population of the three is in line with previous findings (Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Linneberg-Agerholm et al., 2019.

claim: hEPSC-ACL may represent a highly heterogenous population of cells.
source: Although hEPSC-ACL are more similar to the definitive endoderm relative to extra-embryonic endoderm, they are not as similar to the definitive endoderm as hESC-ACL are, perhaps due to hEPSC-ACL representing a highly heterogenous population of cells.
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis to explain the experimental results.

claim: Rset-ACL were the most similar to the extra-embryonic endoderm, making them a potential candidate for modelling the human yolk sac.
source: Rset-ACL were the most similar to the extra-embryonic endoderm, making them a potential candidate for modelling the human yolk sac.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Commitment to a definitive endoderm fate follows an initial intermediate mesendoderm fate.
source: Commitment to a definitive endoderm fate follows an initial intermediate mesendoderm fate (Kimelman and Griffin, 2000), whereas extra-embryonic endoderm derives directly from the ICM without this intermediate state (Niakan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimelman and Griffin, 2000 and Niakan et al., 2012.

claim: Extra-embryonic endoderm derives directly from the ICM without an intermediate mesendoderm state.
source: Commitment to a definitive endoderm fate follows an initial intermediate mesendoderm fate (Kimelman and Griffin, 2000), whereas extra-embryonic endoderm derives directly from the ICM without this intermediate state (Niakan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Niakan et al., 2012.

claim: There is a trend of increase in BRACHYURY expression in hESC-ACL and hEPSC-ACL populations around day 2 of treatment, which then diminished by day 4 in both cases.
source: This revealed a trend of increase in BRACHYURY expression in hESC-ACL and hEPSC-ACL populations around day 2 of treatment, which then diminished by day 4 in both cases.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of BRACHYURY expression dynamics during ACL treatment.

claim: In Rset hPSCs, the trend of BRACHYURY levels observed in hESC-ACL and hEPSC-ACL was not observed.
source: However, in Rset hPSCs, this trend of BRACHYURY levels was not observed.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of BRACHYURY expression dynamics during ACL treatment.

claim: Of the three cell types, the specification dynamics of Rset hPSCs in response to ACL was the most similar to that expected of extra-embryonic endoderm specification.
source: This shows that of the three cell types, the specification dynamics of Rset hPSCs in response to ACL was the most similar to that expected of extra-embryonic endoderm specification.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the BRACHYURY expression dynamics data.

claim: Both hEPSC-ACL and Rset-ACL were able to contribute to the primitive endoderm of mouse embryos.
source: We observed that both hEPSC-ACL and Rset-ACL were able to contribute to the primitive endoderm of mouse embryos (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: hEPSC-ACLs and Rset-ACLs contributed to the mouse primitive endoderm in 18% and 12% of chimeras, respectively.
source: hEPSC-ACLs and Rset-ACLs contributed to the mouse primitive endoderm in 18% and 12% of chimeras, respectively, with hEPSC-ACL contributing to both the epiblast and the primitive endoderm 3% of the time, suggesting a degree of fate plasticity (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: hEPSC-ACL contributed to both the epiblast and the primitive endoderm 3% of the time, suggesting a degree of fate plasticity.
source: hEPSC-ACLs and Rset-ACLs contributed to the mouse primitive endoderm in 18% and 12% of chimeras, respectively, with hEPSC-ACL contributing to both the epiblast and the primitive endoderm 3% of the time, suggesting a degree of fate plasticity (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F, with an interpretation about fate plasticity.

claim: hEPSCs and Rset hPSCs both almost solely contribute to the epiblast compartment within human-mouse chimeric blastocysts.
source: This contribution profile of hEPSC-ACL and Rset-ACL contrasts that of hEPSCs and Rset hPSCs which both almost solely contribute to the epiblast compartment within human-mouse chimeric blastocysts: hEPSCs and Rset hPSCs contribute to the epiblast in 44% and 81% of embryos, and to both the epiblast and primitive endoderm 6% and 4% of the time, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Primed hESCs treated with ACL could not contribute to mouse primitive endoderm.
source: Primed hESCs treated with ACL could not contribute to mouse primitive endoderm (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Based on the transcriptional and functional evidence, Rset-ACL are the most similar to human extra-embryonic endoderm relative to the other two cell lines.
source: Collectively, based on the transcriptional and functional evidence, we concluded that Rset-ACL are the most similar to human extra-embryonic endoderm relative to the other two cell lines.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the transcriptional and functional data.

claim: Despite hEPSC-ACL being able to contribute to the murine primitive endoderm, they also share significant similarities to the definitive endoderm, both in terms of their developmental pathway and transcriptional profile.
source: Despite hEPSC-ACL being able to contribute to the murine primitive endoderm, and thereby sharing some functional properties with the extra-embryonic endoderm, they also share significant similarities to the definitive endoderm, both in terms of their developmental pathway and transcriptional profile.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The high degree of heterogeneity present in hEPSC-ACL cultures is likely the reason they share similarities with both extra-embryonic and definitive endoderm.
source: This is likely due to the high degree of heterogeneity present in hEPSC-ACL cultures.
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis to explain the experimental results.

claim: hESC-ACL are more similar to definitive endoderm, functionally, transcriptionally, and in terms of their developmental trajectory.
source: hESC-ACL are more similar to definitive endoderm, functionally, transcriptionally, and in terms of their developmental trajectory.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Rset-ACL were the most promising candidate for modelling the human yolk sac.
source: Based on these findings we concluded that Rset-ACL were the most promising candidate for modelling the human yolk sac.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Of the 26,510 genes examined, 25,496 were shared between pre-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm (E6–7) and post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm (E10–14).
source: Of the 26,510 genes examined, 25,496 were shared, with 397 and 617 genes being differentially upregulated in the pre- or post-implantation state, respectively (Figure 4A) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 397 genes were differentially upregulated in the pre-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm state.
source: Of the 26,510 genes examined, 25,496 were shared, with 397 and 617 genes being differentially upregulated in the pre- or post-implantation state, respectively (Figure 4A) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 617 genes were differentially upregulated in the post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm state.
source: Of the 26,510 genes examined, 25,496 were shared, with 397 and 617 genes being differentially upregulated in the pre- or post-implantation state, respectively (Figure 4A) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: AXL, a visceral endoderm marker in the mouse, was among the identified markers of post-implantation yolk sac.
source: Interestingly, AXL, a visceral endoderm marker in the mouse (McDonald et al., 2014), was among the identified markers of post-implantation yolk sac (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 3, and a citation to McDonald et al., 2014.

claim: The presence of APOA2 and APOB in the top differentially expressed post-implantation genes alludes to the yolk sac as the primary site of apolipoprotein synthesis in the early embryo.
source: The presence of APOA2 and APOB in the top differentially expressed post-implantation genes once again alludes to the yolk sac as the primary site of apolipoprotein synthesis in the early embryo.
evidence: This claim is presented as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Rset-ACL is the most similar to the post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm.
source: This analysis revealed Rset-ACL to be the most similar to the post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm, while T2iLGö-PrE were more similar to the pre-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: T2iLGö-PrE were more similar to the pre-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm.
source: This analysis revealed Rset-ACL to be the most similar to the post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm, while T2iLGö-PrE were more similar to the pre-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Rset-ACL is the best candidate for modelling yolk sac-epiblast interactions.
source: These results indicate that Rset-ACL is the best candidate for modelling yolk sac-epiblast interactions.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The yolk sac of the mouse embryo harbours an asymmetrically localised subpopulation of cells called the AVE.
source: The yolk sac of the mouse embryo harbours an asymmetrically localised subpopulation of cells called the AVE.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge about mouse embryo development.

claim: The AVE cells secrete inhibitors of BMP, WNT, and NODAL signalling, thereby creating a signalling gradient across the post-implantation epiblast.
source: These cells secrete inhibitors of BMP, WNT, and NODAL signalling, thereby creating a signalling gradient across the post-implantation epiblast.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge about mouse embryo development.

claim: The signalling gradient created by the AVE determines the positioning of the primitive streak and, therefore, the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo.
source: This gradient in turn determines the positioning of the primitive streak and, therefore, the anterior-posterior axis of the embryo (Arnold and Robertson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arnold and Robertson, 2009.

claim: The post-implantation hypoblast of both the cynomolgus monkey and human embryo expresses DKK1, CER1, and NOG.
source: The post-implantation hypoblast of both the cynomolgus monkey and human embryo also expresses DKK1, CER1, and NOG (Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016; Sasaki et al., 2016) and studies of human embryos cultured to post-implantation stages in vitro have suggested that an anterior subpopulation of cells within the human hypoblast may influence BMP signalling within the adjacent epiblast (Molè et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016; Sasaki et al., 2016.

claim: Studies of human embryos cultured to post-implantation stages in vitro have suggested that an anterior subpopulation of cells within the human hypoblast may influence BMP signalling within the adjacent epiblast.
source: The post-implantation hypoblast of both the cynomolgus monkey and human embryo also expresses DKK1, CER1, and NOG (Molè et al., 2021; Nakamura et al., 2016; Sasaki et al., 2016) and studies of human embryos cultured to post-implantation stages in vitro have suggested that an anterior subpopulation of cells within the human hypoblast may influence BMP signalling within the adjacent epiblast (Molè et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Molè et al., 2021.

claim: The human yolk sac may harbour AVE-like cells.
source: This implies that the human yolk sac may harbour AVE-like cells.
evidence: This claim is presented as an inference based on the expression of signaling inhibitors in the human hypoblast.

claim: DKK1, CER1, LEFTY2, and SFRP1 are expressed at greater levels in post-implantation relative to pre-implantation hypoblast.
source: We, therefore, analysed the expression of these pathway inhibitors within the hypoblast of the pre- and post-implantation human embryo using published datasets (Molè et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019) and found that DKK1, CER1, LEFTY2, and SFRP1 are expressed at greater levels in post-implantation relative to pre-implantation hypoblast, while NOG is expressed at higher levels in the pre-implantation hypoblast (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, using published datasets from Molè et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: NOG is expressed at higher levels in the pre-implantation hypoblast.
source: We, therefore, analysed the expression of these pathway inhibitors within the hypoblast of the pre- and post-implantation human embryo using published datasets (Molè et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019) and found that DKK1, CER1, LEFTY2, and SFRP1 are expressed at greater levels in post-implantation relative to pre-implantation hypoblast, while NOG is expressed at higher levels in the pre-implantation hypoblast (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, using published datasets from Molè et al., 2021; Xiang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: All of the analysed inhibitors were upregulated in YSLCs.
source: Given that YSLCs share transcriptional similarity to the post-implantation extra-embryonic endoderm, we examined the expression of WNT and BMP inhibitors in YSLCs and observed that all of the analysed inhibitors were upregulated in YSLCs (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: In human stem cell models, DKK1 and NOG act as WNT and BMP inhibitors, respectively.
source: In human stem cell models, DKK1 and NOG act as WNT and BMP inhibitors, respectively (Martyn et al., 2019; Simunovic et al., 2019), whereas CER1 antagonises both NODAL and BMP signalling in other systems (Aykul and Martinez-Hackert, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martyn et al., 2019 and Simunovic et al., 2019.

claim: CER1 antagonises both NODAL and BMP signalling in other systems.
source: In human stem cell models, DKK1 and NOG act as WNT and BMP inhibitors, respectively (Martyn et al., 2019; Simunovic et al., 2019), whereas CER1 antagonises both NODAL and BMP signalling in other systems (Aykul and Martinez-Hackert, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aykul and Martinez-Hackert, 2016.

claim: YSLCs may share functional characteristics with the mouse AVE and the human anterior hypoblast in their ability to govern cell fate via BMP and WNT inhibition.
source: We, therefore, postulated that YSLCs may share functional characteristics with the mouse AVE and the human anterior hypoblast in their ability to govern cell fate via BMP and WNT inhibition.
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis based on the expression of signaling inhibitors in YSLCs.

claim: hESCs lose their pluripotent character in a BMP-dependent manner when cultured in a 3D 'sandwich' matrix of Geltrex.
source: hESCs have been shown to lose their pluripotent character in a BMP-dependent manner when cultured in a 3D 'sandwich' matrix of Geltrex, in which cells are plated on top of a base layer of Geltrex before being covered by mTESR1 containing 5% Geltrex (Shao et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shao et al., 2017b.

claim: At a density of 60,000 cells per cm2 hESCs lost SOX2 expression and either formed squamous spheroids or lost structural integrity in 3D Geltrex.
source: Confirming these previous findings, we found that at a density of 60,000 cells per cm2 hESCs lost SOX2 expression and either formed squamous spheroids or lost structural integrity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inhibiting WNT signalling using either IWR1 (10 ng ml−1) or XAV (10 ng ml−1) in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex prevented downregulation of SOX2.
source: Similarly, we found that inhibiting WNT signalling using either IWR1 (10 ng ml−1) or XAV (10 ng ml−1) in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex prevented downregulation of SOX2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: hESCs lose SOX2 in 3D Geltrex in response to BMP and WNT signalling pathway activation.
source: Collectively, this indicates that hESCs lose SOX2 in 3D Geltrex in response to BMP and WNT signalling pathway activation.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: SOX2 levels were higher in co-culture conditions of YSLCs and hESCs relative to control hESCs.
source: To test whether YSLCs could antagonise this signalling, YSLCs were cultured at a 1:1 ratio with hESCs for 72 hr in mTeSR1 PLUS, revealing SOX2 levels to be higher in co-culture conditions relative to control hESCs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from co-culture experiments.

claim: There was a slight (but not significant) increase in the number of epithelial spheroids (squamous and columnar) relative to disorganised structures in co-culture conditions of YSLCs and hESCs.
source: We also noted a slight (but not significant) increase in the number of epithelial spheroids (squamous and columnar) relative to disorganised structures in co-culture conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: YSLCs have an ability to inhibit the loss of SOX2 in hESCs that would otherwise occur in 3D Geltrex.
source: This demonstrates an ability of YSLCs to inhibit the loss of SOX2 in hESCs that would otherwise occur in 3D Geltrex.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the co-culture experimental data.

claim: mTeSR1 PLUS conditioned on YSLCs blocked the downregulation of SOX2 within hESCs relative to control conditions.
source: hESCs were then cultured in this conditioned medium for 72 hr in 3D Geltrex. mTeSR1 PLUS conditioned on YSLCs blocked the downregulation of SOX2 within hESCs relative to control conditions and also significantly supported a columnar epithelial morphology (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: mTeSR1 PLUS conditioned on YSLCs significantly supported a columnar epithelial morphology in hESCs.
source: hESCs were then cultured in this conditioned medium for 72 hr in 3D Geltrex. mTeSR1 PLUS conditioned on YSLCs blocked the downregulation of SOX2 within hESCs relative to control conditions and also significantly supported a columnar epithelial morphology (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: YSLCs are able to prevent SOX2 downregulation and support columnar spheroid formation in hESCs in 3D Geltrex via secreted components.
source: These results show that YSLCs are able to prevent SOX2 downregulation and support columnar spheroid formation in hESCs in 3D Geltrex via secreted components, but that the potency of this effect is limited when they are physically co-cultured with hESCs, likely due to a reduced viability of YSLCs in 3D Geltrex conditions.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the conditioned medium experimental data.

claim: The potency of YSLC's effect on hESCs is limited when they are physically co-cultured with hESCs, likely due to a reduced viability of YSLCs in 3D Geltrex conditions.
source: These results show that YSLCs are able to prevent SOX2 downregulation and support columnar spheroid formation in hESCs in 3D Geltrex via secreted components, but that the potency of this effect is limited when they are physically co-cultured with hESCs, likely due to a reduced viability of YSLCs in 3D Geltrex conditions.
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis to explain the experimental results.

claim: Both WNT and BMP pathways were active in mTESR1 PLUS control conditions in 3D hESC spheroids.
source: To understand whether YSLC conditioned medium was inhibiting BMP and WNT signalling within the 3D hESC spheroids, we analysed the levels of the downstream WNT and BMP effectors LEF1 and pSMAD1/5, respectively, in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex in either mTESR1 PLUS or mTESR1 PLUS conditioned on YSLCs. This revealed that both pathways were active in mTESR1 PLUS control conditions, but their activity decreased in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F–H.

claim: WNT and BMP pathway activity decreased in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium in 3D hESC spheroids.
source: To understand whether YSLC conditioned medium was inhibiting BMP and WNT signalling within the 3D hESC spheroids, we analysed the levels of the downstream WNT and BMP effectors LEF1 and pSMAD1/5, respectively, in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex in either mTESR1 PLUS or mTESR1 PLUS conditioned on YSLCs. This revealed that both pathways were active in mTESR1 PLUS control conditions, but their activity decreased in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F–H.

claim: Addition of 1 ng ml−1 of BMP4 to mTeSR1 PLUS led to a marked decrease in SOX2 expression concomitant with an increase in the levels of nuclear pSMAD1/5 in hESCs.
source: Addition of 1 ng ml−1 of BMP4 to mTeSR1 PLUS led to a marked decrease in SOX2 expression concomitant with an increase in the levels of nuclear pSMAD1/5 (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I,J.

claim: When hESCs were exposed to BMP4 in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium, SOX2 expression did not significantly decrease and levels of nuclear pSMAD1/5 remained low.
source: Strikingly, when hESCs were exposed to BMP4 in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium, SOX2 expression did not significantly decrease and levels of nuclear pSMAD1/5 remained low (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I,J.

claim: When hESCs were cultured in the presence of 1 μg ml−1 WNT3A they lost SOX2 expression and upregulated LEF1.
source: Similarly, when hESCs were cultured in the presence of 1 μg ml−1 WNT3A they lost SOX2 expression and upregulated LEF1 (Figure 5K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K,L.

claim: When hESCs were cultured in the presence of 1 μg ml−1 WNT3a and YSLC conditioned medium, the downregulation of SOX2 and upregulation of LEF1 was significantly counteracted.
source: However, when hESCs were cultured in the presence of 1 μg ml−1 WNT3a and YSLC conditioned medium, the downregulation of SOX2 and upregulation of LEF1 was significantly counteracted (Figure 5K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K–L.

claim: A similar trend was observed for NANOG levels in hESCs that were exposed to either BMP4 or WNT3a in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium.
source: A similar trend was observed for NANOG levels in hESCs that were exposed to either BMP4 or WNT3a in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–K.

claim: YSLCs block loss of pluripotent gene expression by antagonising WNT and BMP signalling via secreted factors and can thereby influence hESC fate.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that YSLCs block loss of pluripotent gene expression by antagonising WNT and BMP signalling via secreted factors and can thereby influence hESC fate.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Within the mouse embryo, the AVE acts to induce anterior fate and repress the formation of the primitive streak in the epiblast cells adjacent to it.
source: Within the mouse embryo, the AVE acts to induce anterior fate and repress the formation of the primitive streak in the epiblast cells adjacent to it (Rivera-Pérez and Hadjantonakis, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rivera-Pérez and Hadjantonakis, 2015.

claim: A similar function has been recently proposed for the human anterior hypoblast.
source: A similar function has been recently proposed for the human anterior hypoblast (Molè et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Molè et al., 2021.

claim: YSLCs may bear similarity to both the mouse AVE and the human anterior hypoblast, and may be able to prevent hESCs from differentiating into posterior epiblast fates.
source: Given the ability of YSLCs to influence hESC fate via WNT and BMP inhibition, we hypothesised that YSLCs may bear similarity to both the mouse AVE and the human anterior hypoblast, and may, therefore, be able to prevent hESCs from differentiating into posterior epiblast fates.
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claim: In control conditions, BRACHYURY was not induced in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex, while GATA6 was upregulated.
source: Consequently, we analysed the expression of the posterior markers BRACHYURY and GATA6 in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex. In control conditions, BRACHYURY was not induced, while GATA6 was upregulated, and this upregulation was blocked in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: GATA6 upregulation in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex was blocked in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium.
source: Consequently, we analysed the expression of the posterior markers BRACHYURY and GATA6 in hESCs cultured in 3D Geltrex. In control conditions, BRACHYURY was not induced, while GATA6 was upregulated, and this upregulation was blocked in the presence of YSLC conditioned medium (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: YSLC conditioned medium suppressed the upregulation of BRACHYURY while also preventing the loss of SOX2 in hESCs cultured in mesoderm induction medium.
source: Next, to test whether YSLCs can block mesoderm specification, we employed a 2D mesoderm induction protocol involving the supplementation of 10 ng µl−1 BMP4 to hESCs for 3 days (Richter et al., 2014). Strikingly, immunofluorescence analyses revealed that YSLC conditioned medium suppressed the upregulation of BRACHYURY while also preventing the loss of SOX2 in hESCs cultured in mesoderm induction medium (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–F, with a citation to Richter et al., 2014 for the mesoderm induction protocol.

claim: GATA6 was upregulated in hESCs after BMP4 treatment and this was countered by YSLC conditioned medium.
source: GATA6 was also upregulated in hESCs after BMP4 treatment and this was also countered by YSLC conditioned medium.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the mesoderm induction experiments.

claim: YSLC conditioned medium suppressed the upregulation of the posterior markers EOMES, SOX17, MIXL1, FOXA2, and GSC at the RNA level in hESCs cultured in mesoderm induction medium.
source: Similarly, YSLC conditioned medium suppressed the upregulation of the posterior markers EOMES, SOX17, MIXL1, FOXA2, and GSC at the RNA level (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: YSLCs are able to inhibit posterior epiblast marker expression in hESCs.
source: These results, therefore, demonstrate that YSLCs are able to inhibit posterior epiblast marker expression in hESCs.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Expression of both OCT4 and NANOG was higher in hESCs cultured in YSLC conditioned medium at all timepoints relative to control mTeSR conditions.
source: This revealed that expression of both OCT4 and NANOG was higher in hESCs cultured in YSLC conditioned medium at all timepoints relative to control mTeSR conditions, while SOX2 levels were significantly different from day 3 of culture (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: SOX2 levels were significantly different from day 3 of culture in hESCs cultured in YSLC conditioned medium relative to control mTeSR conditions.
source: This revealed that expression of both OCT4 and NANOG was higher in hESCs cultured in YSLC conditioned medium at all timepoints relative to control mTeSR conditions, while SOX2 levels were significantly different from day 3 of culture (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: SOX1 levels steadily increased relative to controls over the 5-day culture period but were downregulated after 7 days in hESCs cultured in YSLC conditioned medium.
source: SOX1 levels steadily increased relative to controls over the 5-day culture period but were downregulated after 7 days (Figure 7C and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: OTX2 expression did not increase until day 3, and peaked at day 4, before decreasing again in hESCs cultured in YSLC conditioned medium.
source: Conversely, OTX2 expression did not increase until day 3, and peaked at day 4, before decreasing again (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: In the presence of conditioned medium, pluripotency markers and anterior ectoderm markers were co-expressed in hESCs.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of conditioned medium, pluripotency markers and anterior ectoderm markers were co-expressed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YSLCs can upregulate pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers in hESCs in 3D.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that YSLCs can upregulate pluripotency and anterior ectoderm markers in hESCs in 3D.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: After the completion of the 15-day neural differentiation protocol using YSLC conditioned medium, the anterior ectoderm markers SOX1, PAX6, NESTIN, and NOTCH1 were all significantly upregulated in hESCs.
source: After the completion of the 15-day protocol, the anterior ectoderm markers SOX1, PAX6, NESTIN, and NOTCH1 were all significantly upregulated in hESCs (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F–H.

claim: SOX2 was downregulated relative from controls, but was still present, as has been observed during the early stages of neural specification.
source: SOX2 was downregulated relative from controls, but was still present, as has been observed during the early stages of neural specification (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: YSLC conditioned medium induced the upregulation of anterior ectoderm markers to intermediate levels relative to hESCs cultured in dual SMAD conditions and control hESCs.
source: Interestingly, YSLC conditioned medium induced the upregulation of anterior ectoderm markers to intermediate levels relative to hESCs cultured in dual SMAD conditions and control hESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: YSLCs support anterior ectoderm marker expression in combination with pluripotency markers.
source: Overall these results demonstrate that YSLCs support anterior ectoderm marker expression in combination with pluripotency markers and, therefore, share functional similarities with the mammalian AVE.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: YSLCs share functional similarities with the mammalian AVE.
source: Overall these results demonstrate that YSLCs support anterior ectoderm marker expression in combination with pluripotency markers and, therefore, share functional similarities with the mammalian AVE.
evidence: This claim is presented as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
